nameStory: The short-winged meadow katydid gets its name from its notably stubby wings that don't extend much past its body, unlike many of its long-winged relatives. While most katydids are known for their impressive wing spans, this little meadow dweller traded flying ability for a more ground-hugging lifestyle. The 'meadow' part of its name reflects its preferred grassland habitat where it spends most of its time hopping rather than flying.
description: The short-winged meadow katydid is a small, green grasshopper-like insect that's more closely related to crickets than true grasshoppers. These slender insects typically measure about an inch long and have distinctively short wings that barely cover half their abdomen. Their bright green coloration helps them blend perfectly into grass and low vegetation. Unlike their musical katydid cousins that call from trees, these little meadow dwellers stay close to the ground in grassy areas.

idTips.label: Short Wings
idTips.description: Wings that stop well short of the abdomen tip, covering only about half the body length - you can clearly see the exposed green abdomen segments beyond the wing tips

idTips.label: Bright Green Color
idTips.description: Vibrant grass-green coloration all over the body that looks almost artificial in its intensity, helping it disappear completely in green grass

idTips.label: Long Antennae
idTips.description: Thread-like antennae that are longer than the body and constantly twitch and wave as the insect explores its surroundings

idTips.label: Slender Build
idTips.description: Narrow, delicate body shape that feels surprisingly light if gently handled, quite different from the chunky build of grasshoppers

idTips.label: Ground Behavior
idTips.description: Tends to hop short distances through grass rather than fly, and when disturbed will often crawl down into thick vegetation rather than take flight

habitat: Look for short-winged meadow katydids in open grassy areas including meadows, old fields, prairie remnants, and unmowed areas along roadsides. They prefer areas with dense grass cover and are often found in slightly damp meadows or the edges of wetlands where the grass grows thick. You'll rarely find them in wooded areas, instead seeking out sunny, open spaces with plenty of grass and low herbaceous plants.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active; eggs laid the previous fall are developing in the soil and plant stems.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity begins in mid to late summer when adults emerge and begin calling. Listen for their high-pitched buzzing songs on warm evenings.
seasonality.fall: Most active period for adults, with mating and egg-laying occurring. Their green color may start to fade slightly as the season progresses.
seasonality.winter: Adults have died off and the species overwinters as eggs hidden in plant stems and soil, waiting for spring warmth to hatch.

funFact: Short-winged meadow katydids are musical minimalists - while their tree-dwelling katydid cousins create the classic 'katy-did' chorus, these meadow specialists produce a continuous high-pitched buzz that sounds more like a tiny electric motor running, and they often sing during the day rather than just at night!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other meadow katydid species, but the short wings are the dead giveaway - if you can see lots of green abdomen sticking out past the wing tips, you've found the short-winged species. Remember: 'Short wings, long green behind' to distinguish it from its longer-winged meadow cousins.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called katydids, meadow katydids like this one rarely make the classic 'katy-did' sound that gave the family its name. That famous call comes from the larger, tree-dwelling true katydids. This can be confusing for beginners who expect all katydids to sound the same!
compareHints: Among its meadow katydid relatives, the short-winged species is immediately recognizable by its abbreviated wings - all other Conocephalus species in New England have long wings that extend to or beyond the tip of their abdomen. The slender meadow katydid and straight-lanced meadow katydid both have full-length wings and are more likely to be found higher up in vegetation rather than staying close to the ground.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's meadow katydids, the slender meadow katydid lives up to its name with the thinnest, most elongated body of the group.

Among New England's meadow katydids, the straight-lanced stands out for its perfectly straight wing edges - the short-winged has wings that don't extend past its body, the slender has curved wing edges, and the saltmarsh is found only in coastal salt marshes.

Unlike the Short-winged Meadow Katydid which has reduced wings and prefers wet meadows, or the Slender Meadow Katydid found in freshwater marshes, the Saltmarsh Meadow Katydid is distinguished by its exclusive salt marsh habitat and well-developed wings.
